t:
(a) 
Duties of Secretaries.—This title shall be enforced by the Secretary of Commerce and the Secretary of the department in which the Coast Guard is operating. Such Secretaries may by agreement utilize, on a reimbursable basis or otherwise, the personnel, services, equipment (including aircraft and vessels), and facilities of any other Federal agency, or of any State agency, in the performance of such duties. Such Secretaries shall, and the head of any Federal or State agency that has entered into an agreement with either such Secretary under this section may (if the agreement so provides), authorize officers to enforce the provisions of this title or any regulation or permit issued under this title.
 
    (b) 
District Court Jurisdiction.—The district courts of the United States shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any case or controversy arising under the provisions of this title. In the case of Guam, and any Commonwealth, territory, or possession of the United States in the Pacific Ocean, the appropriate court is the United States District Court for the District of Guam, except that in the case of American Samoa, the appropriate court is the United States District Court for the District of Hawaii.
 
    (c) 
Powers of Enforcement Officers.—

        (1) 
Any officer who is authorized under subsection (a) to enforce the provisions of this title may—

            (A) 
with or without a warrant or other process—

                (i) 
arrest any person, if the officer has reasonable cause to believe that such person has committed an act prohibited by paragraph (6), (7), (8), or (9) of section 106;
 
                (ii) 
board, and search or inspect, any high seas fishing vessel;
 
                (iii) 
seize any high seas fishing vessel (together with its fishing gear, furniture, appurtenances, stores, and cargo) used or employed in, or with respect to which it reasonably appears that such vessel was used  or employed in, the violation of any provision of this title or any regulation or permit issued under this title;
 
                (iv) 
seize any living marine resource (wherever found) taken or retained, in any manner, in connection with or as a result of the commission of any act prohibited by section 106;
 
                (v) 
seize any other evidence related to any violation of any provision of this title or any regulation or permit issued under this title;
  
            (B) 
execute any warrant or other process issued by any court of competent jurisdiction; and
 
            (C) 
exercise any other lawful authority.
  
        (2) 
Subject to the direction of the Secretary, a person charged with law enforcement responsibilities by the Secretary who is performing a duty related to enforcement of a law regarding fisheries or other marine resources may make an arrest without a warrant for an offense against the United States committed in his presence, or for a felony cognizable under the laws of the United States, if he has reasonable grounds to believe that the person to be arrested has committed or is committing a felony.
  
    (d) 
Issuance of Citations.—If any authorized officer finds that a high seas fishing vessel is operating or has been operated in violation of any provision of this title, such officer may issue a citation to the owner or operator of such vessel in lieu of proceeding under subsection (c). If a permit has been issued pursuant to this title for such vessel, such officer shall note the issuance of any citation under this subsection, including the date thereof and the reason therefor, on the permit. The Secretary shall maintain  a record of all citations issued pursuant to this subsection.
 
    (e) 
Liability for Costs.—Any person assessed a civil penalty for, or convicted of, any violation of this Act shall be liable for the cost incurred in storage, care, and maintenance of any living marine resource or other property seized in connection with the violation.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that agreements with State agencies amount to coordination with outside parties, and that the district court provision grants a right to sue. But the agreements only borrow State personnel and equipment to carry out enforcement; they do not consult States before a federal policy decision. Subsection (b) merely allocates jurisdiction and venue, which the definition treats as a trap rather than a grant of a right to challenge a federal decision. The rest covers enforcement powers, citations and cost liability, with no comment period, hearing, advisory body or rulemaking mandate.
fable.s: Such Secretaries may by agreement utilize, on a reimbursable basis or otherwise, the personnel, services, equipment (including aircraft and vessels), and facilities of any other Federal agency, or of any State agency, in the performance of such duties.

qwen_block.w: This section outlines enforcement mechanisms, including the authority of federal and state officers to arrest and seize property, and establishes the jurisdiction of federal district courts. It does not require consultation with outside parties, public comment periods, or advisory boards before a decision is made. The mention of court jurisdiction falls under the 'No' trap for describing litigation procedures rather than granting a right to participate in the decision-making process itself.
qwen_block.s: The district courts of the United States shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any case or controversy arising under the provisions of this title.

opus.w: The section sets up enforcement duties and powers. The only outside party is a State agency, and it can only lend personnel, equipment and facilities to help enforce the law; it is not consulted before any federal decision. The district-court provision only says which court hears cases, which is a listed trap, and the mention of regulations and permits points to rules made elsewhere rather than granting rulemaking authority.
opus.s: Such Secretaries may by agreement utilize, on a reimbursable basis or otherwise, the personnel, services, equipment (including aircraft and vessels), and facilities of any other Federal agency, or of any State agency, in the performance of such duties.
opus.b:
1. **Tempting readings:** Several parts of this section look like participation at first glance. The Secretaries may make agreements with State agencies. The section gives district courts jurisdiction. It also mentions "any regulation or permit issued under this title."
2. **Why they fail:** None of these brings an outside party into a federal decision.
   - The State-agency agreements only borrow State personnel and equipment to enforce the law. States are not consulted before any decision is made.
   - Granting court jurisdiction is a listed trap. It is not the same as giving an outside party a right to sue over a decision.
   - The reference to regulations just points to rules made elsewhere. It does not create rulemaking authority here.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines enforcement powers (arrest, seizure) and court jurisdiction. Enforcement actions against private parties are not 'participation' as defined (consultation/coordination before a decision). Granting court jurisdiction is explicitly excluded from the definition of participation, which distinguishes it from granting a right to sue over a decision. There is no mention of public comment periods, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with outside entities prior to federal decisions.
qwen_chat.s: (b) District Court Jurisdiction.—The district courts of the United States shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any case or controversy arising under the provisions of this title.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the ability of enforcement officers to arrest, search, or seize vessels involves interaction with private parties (fishermen, vessel owners), and thus constitutes "participation." However, this is incorrect because these are enforcement actions (police powers) taken *against* outside parties, not a process where outside parties consult with or coordinate with the government *before* a decision is made. The definition of participation requires consultation, coordination, advisory roles, or the right to sue/object *before* or *during* the decision-making process, not post-violation enforcement. Additionally, subsection (b) grants jurisdiction to courts, but as per the definition, "a court's jurisdiction... is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision."
